c.tagline: Riviera Maya's beach-and-nightlife capital, where Quinta Avenida meets the Caribbean.

taxi.fareNote: Playa's taxis are unmetered and run by a strong union, so agree the fare before getting in as rates are zone-based and rise at night. Uber and DiDi operate but sit in a legal grey area, with taxi-union tension sometimes restricting app pickups at the ADO terminal and beach clubs.

emergency.note: 911 is Mexico's unified emergency number for police, fire, and ambulance; 078 is the national tourist assistance line.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_landmark.Centro (Downtown / Quinta Avenida): Quinta Avenida (5th Avenue), Playa del Carmen
hood_landmark.Playacar: Playacar beach and golf club, Playa del Carmen

avoid.reason: Tourist strip safe; caution off 5th Avenue at night; occasional cartel-related incidents — avoid drugs

hood_desc: The walkable heart of Playa built around Quinta Avenida (5th Ave), the pedestrian strip packed with restaurants, bars, shops and the Cozumel ferry pier; best for first-timers who want everything and the beach within a few blocks.

An upscale gated community just south of Centro with all-inclusive resorts, an 18-hole golf course, quiet tree-lined streets and calm beaches; suits families and travelers wanting security and resort comfort.

The polished beachside strip north of Constituyentes Avenue with boutique hotels, rooftop bars and beach clubs between Quinta Avenida and the sand; good for style-minded visitors who want to walk to nightlife and the water.

A calmer residential-beach neighborhood at the north end of town with the quiet, snorkel-friendly Coco Beach and easy access to Centro; ideal for a relaxed stay near the water without the party crowds.
A gritty, up-and-coming local barrio inland and north of Centro with affordable apartments, taquerias and an authentic non-touristy feel; suits budget travelers and long-stay nomads.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water only; resorts filter theirs.

transit.hours: Colectivos and city buses run roughly 5:00am to 11:00pm; ADO intercity coaches and ride apps fill later hours, and the compact Centro is easily walked.
transit.note: Playa del Carmen has no metro, tram, or rail transit; getting around means shared colectivo vans (mainly the Highway 307 corridor to Tulum and Cancun), local city buses, taxis, and ride apps, while Centro and Quinta Avenida are best explored on foot.
transit.pay: Colectivos and city buses are paid in cash to the driver (roughly MXN 15-45 by distance); there is no rechargeable transit card. ADO intercity coaches are ticketed at the terminal or online.

bus: ADO bus terminal (Calle 5 / Quinta Avenida, first-class intercity coaches)
ferry: Ultramar & Winjet ferries to Cozumel (Playa del Carmen pier)

transit.m: ADO airport bus (Cancun Airport to Playa del Carmen ADO terminal, ~1 hr)
Authorized airport taxi/van to Playa Centro, ~50-60 min

tip.r: Around 10-15% at restaurants is customary; tip bartenders, tour guides and beach-club staff in cash, and note some resorts add a service charge.

food.name: Tacos al pastor
food.desc: Chile-marinated pork shaved off a vertical trompo, finished with pineapple, onion and cilantro on a small corn tortilla.

places.name: El Fogon
places.note: Playa's most famous taqueria; unpretentious, always packed, and a local benchmark for pastor.

places.name: Taqueria El Nero
places.note: Neighbourhood trompo spot away from Fifth Avenue prices, busy with residents late into the night.

places.name: Super Aki street carts
places.note: Cluster of taco trucks outside the supermarket; the local street-food scene at its most honest.

food.name: Cochinita pibil
food.desc: Achiote-rubbed pork slow-cooked in banana leaf, piled into tacos and tortas with habanero salsa and pickled onion. A Yucatan Peninsula staple.

places.name: La Cochi Loka
places.note: Tiny window-front counter that locals hit for cochinita tacos, panuchos and guisado tacos.

places.name: Mercado Municipal
places.note: Working market fondas serving cochinita and other Yucatecan guisados from early morning.

places.name: El Fogon
places.note: Reliable cochinita tacos and tortas alongside the famous al pastor trompo.

food.name: Tacos de sirloin
food.desc: Playa's own specialty: chopped grilled sirloin on flour or corn tortillas with melted cheese, avocado and a wall of salsas and toppings.

places.name: Don Sirloin
places.note: The name in Playa for sirloin tacos; laid-back, late-night and always crowded with locals.

places.name: El Chuleton
places.note: Unassuming plaza taqueria that foodies rate as the best-value tacos in town.

places.name: Los 7 Reyes
places.note: Local favourite for grilled meat tacos and generous salsa bar at neighbourhood prices.

food.name: Ceviche and aguachile
food.desc: Caribbean fish and shrimp cured in lime; aguachile adds a blast of raw chile and cucumber. Served on tostadas with saltines and cold beer.

places.name: Los Aguachiles
places.note: Casual, loud and hugely popular for aguachile, ceviche tostadas and generous coastal plates.

places.name: El Doctorcito
places.note: Go-to spot for seafood cocktails and aguachile away from the Fifth Avenue tourist run.

places.name: La Floresta
places.note: Outskirts marisqueria known for some of the best fish tacos and shrimp cocktails in Playa.

food.name: Marquesitas
food.desc: Crisp rolled crepe filled with Nutella, cajeta, jam or cream cheese and finished with grated Edam bola cheese. The peninsula's favourite street sweet.

places.name: Parque Fundadores carts
places.note: Evening carts by the church and beach; the easiest place to catch one fresh off the iron.

places.name: Quinta Avenida vendors
places.note: Several stands along the pedestrian street, busiest and freshest after sunset.

places.name: Mercado Municipal
places.note: Local-priced marquesitas among the market food stalls, away from the tourist strip.

food.name: Michelada
food.desc: Mexican lager built over lime, salt and chile sauces in a chile-rimmed glass; the standard beach-heat antidote across Quintana Roo.

places.name: Los Aguachiles
places.note: Micheladas and cold beer are half the point here; pairs with the aguachile and ceviche.

places.name: La Floresta
places.note: Beer-and-seafood local hangout where micheladas arrive in oversized chile-rimmed glasses.

places.name: El Fogon
places.note: Simple, cheap micheladas to go with the taco order; a proper local taqueria experience.

food.name: Agua de horchata
food.desc: Sweet rice-and-cinnamon water served over ice, the traditional cooling partner to spicy tacos. Look for jamaica and tamarindo in the same jars.

places.name: Mercado Municipal
places.note: Market fondas pour house-made aguas frescas by the jar at local prices.

places.name: La Cochi Loka
places.note: Horchata and jamaica to wash down the cochinita tacos, exactly how locals order it.

places.name: El Fogon
places.note: Big pitchers of horchata on every table at Playa's best-known taqueria.

landmarks: Quinta Avenida (Fifth Avenue)
This pedestrian artery runs twenty-plus blocks parallel to the beach, packed with boutiques, taquerias, mezcal bars and people-watching from morning until late.
Parque Fundadores and Portal Maya
The beachfront founders' park frames its soaring bronze Portal Maya sculpture against the Caribbean, with Voladores de Papantla performers spinning at sunset.
Playa Mamitas
Playa del Carmen's liveliest beach pairs powdery sand and turquoise water with fashionable beach clubs, DJs and festival energy nearly year-round.
Xcaret Park
This eco-archaeological mega-park combines underground rivers, sea-turtle pools and Maya ruins with a spectacular 300-performer evening pageant of Mexican history.
Rio Secreto
Helmeted and wet-suited, visitors wade through a stunning underground river system dripping with crystalline stalactites just south of the city.
Cenote Chaak Tun
Stalactite-filled caverns on the town's edge hide glassy turquoise pools where snorkelers glide beneath ancient rock formations lit by shafts of light.
Xaman-Ha Ruins (Playacar)
Modest Maya temples scattered through the Playacar resort district once guarded the departure point for pilgrims canoeing to the shrine of Cozumel.
Capilla de Nuestra Senora del Carmen
This small white chapel beside Parque Fundadores honors the city's patroness and offers a serene, photogenic contrast to Quinta Avenida's bustle.
Punta Esmeralda
Locals favor this northern beach where a shallow freshwater cenote seeps into the sea, creating a natural swimming pool right on the sand.
Coco Bongo
A cabaret-style nightclub near Quinta Avenida known for acrobatic aerial shows, live bands, and celebrity-impersonator acts that run past dawn.

train.note: Mexico has no international passenger trains. The Tren Maya calls at Playa del Carmen on its Yucatan loop, linking Cancun Aeropuerto, Tulum, Merida and on toward Palenque - buy tickets on the official site or at the station.

bus.note: ADO's first-class coaches run from Playa's downtown terminal across the Yucatan and on to Belize City via Chetumal - carry your passport for the border and cash for Belize fees. ADO also covers Cancun, Tulum, Merida and Valladolid.

ferry.note: No international ferries call at Playa. Ultramar and Winjet passenger ferries shuttle across to Cozumel roughly hourly from the pier at the foot of Calle 1, a 30-45 minute crossing.

half.name: Tulum
half.blurb: Cliff-top Maya ruins over a turquoise beach, about 1 hr south along Highway 307.

half.name: Cozumel
half.blurb: Caribbean dive island reached by a 45-min ferry from the Playa pier, ringed by coral reefs.

half.name: Akumal
half.blurb: Calm bay 25 min south famous for swimming with sea turtles over seagrass beds.

half.name: Cenote Dos Ojos
half.blurb: Crystalline freshwater cavern cenotes near Tulum, perfect for snorkeling and cave diving.

full.name: Chichen Itza
full.blurb: The iconic Maya pyramid-city and Wonder of the World, about 3 hrs inland via Valladolid.

full.name: Coba
full.blurb: Jungle-clad Maya ruins with a climbable pyramid, about 1.5 hrs from Playa near Tulum.

full.name: Isla Mujeres
full.blurb: Laid-back island off Cancun with golf-cart lanes and Playa Norte's shallow turquoise water.

full.name: Valladolid
full.blurb: Colorful colonial town and cenote base about 2 hrs inland, a gateway to Chichen Itza.
